source_title: TheLostPantheon/nativ: PS Vita games recompiled into native PC programs: you bring your own games and firmware - GitHub
source_excerpt:
Project Nativ turns PS Vita games into native programs for macOS, Linux and Windows. You bring your own copy of a game. The tools recompile it on your machine, and it runs like any other program, with extras the Vita never had: higher resolutions, wider screens, 60 fps and mouse aiming, depending on the game.
A Vita game is ARM code written against Sony's system software. Nativ handles the two separately.
The game's code is recompiled. A static recompiler translates the game's ARMv7 code, Thumb-2, VFP and NEON included, into C once, ahead of time. That C is compiled into a native program.
The system underneath is rebuilt. Sony's own libraries that a game loads, such as libgxm, libc and FIOS, are recompiled with it from your firmware. Below them, a runtime stands in for the Vita's kernel and hardware: it runs the game's threads, draws its graphics on your GPU and plays its sound.
This repository holds no game code, game data or firmware, and nothing we distribute ever will. You supply your own copy of each game and Sony's firmware update file, and the tools decrypt and recompile them on your machine.
Each game's pack supports exact releases, recognised by the SHA-256 of the game's main program. Game-specific fixes, such as Killzone's physics fix or the widescreen cameras, patch code at fixed addresses, so they only fit the build they were written for. Your game data doesn't need to match; the main program does.
Not supported yet: other regions (EU, JP, Asia) and the later updates of Uncharted (1.03), Unit 13 (1.01) and Shovel Knight (1.08, Treasure Trove). The launcher recognises them and tells you which release it supports. It keeps an unsupported update, and the game runs without it. Porting a new release starts with dev/hookmap.py , which carried 43 of Killzone 1.12's 46 hooks over from 1.00 by matching code.
Players use the launcher. It walks you through first-run setup, then builds and starts your games. Build it with launcher/build.sh ; the result is launcher/nativ .
Developers can run each stage of the pipeline with ./vitarecomp from the top of the checkout. Run it without arguments for the full list.
On Windows, use the Python driver directly from PowerShell instead of the zsh wrapper:
Replace --help with a stage and its arguments. The Windows player release includes its own Python and toolchain; the developer guide describes building that distribution on macOS or Linux.
The pipeline's Python needs the packages in requirements.txt , installed in .venv at the top of the checkout. The Windows player release includes its Python in python/ .
Your games, firmware, licences, builds and saves live in one library folder:
dump/ inside a checkout, which git ignores;
otherwise your per-user data folder: ~/Library/Application Support/ProjectNativ/Nativ/library on macOS, under ~/.local/share on Linux and under %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows;
./vitarecomp dist writes an install that holds only what ships. Running it again over an install it wrote updates the program and leaves your library alone. Two scripts add what a player's machine lacks:
Linux: dev/linux-install.sh adds its own compiler and Python, for machines like the Steam Deck that have neither.
macOS: dev/macos-install.sh adds SDL, SPIRV-Cross, FFmpeg's H.264 decoder and Python, and a Project Nativ.app to start it. The player needs only Apple's Command Line Tools, which the app offers to install. Build the libraries once with runtime/platform/macos/setup-toolchain.sh .
The player guide covers the rest from the player's side: first run, controls, online play and reporting a bug.
Player guide : installing, first run, controls, online play, known issues and bug reports.
How it works : the design, layer by layer.
Working on Nativ : the pipeline, packs and versions, and working across machines.
The runtime in detail : display timing, audio, the GPU backend, controls, hooks and metrics.
Verification : the regression gate and how the translation and renderer are checked.
Debugging a game : logs, captures, replays and the renderer's switches.
Online play : matchmaking, finding other players, and the encrypted links between them.
The shader compiler and the USSE instruction set : the Vita's GPU shaders and how we translate them.
Project Nativ is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE . Third-party code keeps its own licence, and THIRD_PARTY.md lists it with the projects parts of Nativ are ported from.
Nativ contains no Sony or game code. You supply your own games and the firmware from Sony's site; the games are recompiled on your machine and never leave it.
Nativ is made with the help of AI tools: much of its code and documentation was written with AI assistance, under its developer's direction, and tested on the games themselves.
Nativ is free, and everything in it is for everyone. If you'd like to support its development, you can leave a tip on Ko-fi .
